title: Warren defies Schumer as Dem civil war explodes over must-win Senate race
summary: Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders back Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan's Democratic primary, splitting from Chuck Schumer's endorsement of Haley Stevens.
story: Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic candidate for Michigan's U.S. Senate seat, told supporters that ICE, health insurers and corporate interests should see him as "dangerous." (Credit: Youtube/Bernie Sanders)
There’s a battle to shape the Democratic Party this fall, and two top Senate Democrats are taking different paths in their bids to put their mark on the process.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., endorsed Abdul El-Sayed in the duel for the Democratic Senate nomination in Michigan. It’s a break from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who is backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

The diverging endorsements are emblematic of the fight going on behind the scenes and publicly in the Democratic Party as the old guard fights to stand its ground, while a progressive surge threatens to completely overtake the party.
DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Elizabeth Warren conduct a roundtable on housing costs in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 7, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
For example, Warren backed former Maine Senate Democratic nominee Graham Platner, while Schumer had courted and pushed Maine Gov. Janet Mills to get into the race.
And hours after Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., stumped for El-Sayed, Warren jumped into the fray.
In her endorsement video for El-Sayed on Monday, she noted that he was "the only candidate in this race not taking corporate money, and he's fighting to get money out of politics altogether."
MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT MALLORY MCMORROW DROPS OUT OF SENATE RACE WEEKS BEFORE PRIMARY

"And make no mistake," Warren said. "Abdul is the only candidate in this race who can build the grassroots movement needed to win in November. More money in your pocket, to get money out of politics and deliver ‘Medicare-for-all.’ Michigan, let's get this done."

Notably, Warren had previously endorsed Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the race earlier this month. McMorrow was opposed to "Medicare-for-all," a key policy push of Warren’s.

And El-Sayed has made headlines, like Platner, for his old social media posts — particularly his pitch to "defund the police" as a means to reinvest tax dollars to prevent the purchase of "war materiel to wage war in our streets."
WATCH: SURFACED VIDEOS OF DEM SENATE CANDIDATE BACKING 'DEFUND THE POLICE' CONTRADICT RECENT DENIALS
Senate candidate from Michigan Abdul El-Sayed has been endorsed by Bernie Sanders and embraced comparisons between himself and Zohran Mamdani. (Bill Pugliano/Getty Images)
Schumer took his time to go public with his endorsement in what was once a messy, three-way primary battle, first privately backing Stevens.
"I think she has the best chance to win," Schumer told Punchbowl News last month.
Stevens has clinched the backing of a handful of other Senate Democrats, including Sens. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., Chris Coons, D-Del., and Gary Peters, D-Mich., whose seat she’s eying to make her own.
El-Sayed has also amassed a list of heavy hitters, including Warren, Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Neither candidate has committed to backing Schumer to stay as Democratic leader heading into next year’s new session of Congress. And so far, El-Sayed has not spoken with the Senate’s top Democrat.
Instead, he views his candidacy as "a threat" to Schumer and the old guard’s system.

He told Politico that Schumer and Democrats were worried about his plans to push for an end to corporate money entering politics, given that the top Senate Democrat’s "whole approach is that you get to go talk to the money people and then dole out their corporate money to help elect the people who are going to do the things that corporations want."
"So, of course, they’re freaking out," El-Sayed said. "They’re not freaking out because they think I’m going to lose. They’re freaking out because they think I’m going to win."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Socialist-backed Michigan Senate hopeful calls American politics a 'disease' after professing love for US
summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed praised America before arguing the nation's political system is a "disease" and calling for ICE to be abolished.
story: Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic candidate for Michigan's U.S. Senate seat, told supporters that ICE, health insurers and corporate interests should see him as "dangerous." (Credit: Youtube/Bernie Sanders)
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday described America's political system as a "disease" moments after professing his love for the country where he was raised.
El-Sayed delivered blistering attacks on the American political system during the final stop of "The People v. The Powerful" tour at DeVos Performance Hall in Grand Rapids.

He spoke at the event alongside Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., as the trio criticized President Donald Trump, party leaders, corporations and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The Egyptian American physician and former public health official first reflected on the opportunities he said America had afforded him, noting he received an "incredible" public university education and a medical education funded through the National Institutes of Health.
DEM SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED RECOUNTS SMASHING VODKA BOTTLE AFTER BEARD CRITICISM

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Sen. Bernie Sanders speak during the "The People v. The Powerful" campaign event at the Detroit Opera House on July 18, 2026. (Nic Antaya/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"No, don't get it twisted. I love America. I know exactly what America gave to me. I know what my life would have been, but for America," El-Sayed said. "I know what America can do, and at the same time, it's impossible not to reflect on the worst moments of those 250 years as well."
He then argued that Trump was merely a symptom of broader problems in American politics.
"Donald Trump is not, himself, the disease of our politics. He's just the worst symptom of the disease of our politics," El-Sayed said.
"The disease? It's the system that allows corporations and billionaires and special interests like AIPAC to buy and sell politicians to rig the system against us."
Ocasio-Cortez also echoed that message moments prior, telling the crowd, "You deserve a politics that treats the disease and not the symptoms."
BILL MAHER CALLS OUT BERNIE SANDERS, SAYS HE'S TIRED OF HEARING THE RICH DON'T PAY THEIR FAIR SHARE OF TAXES
Michigan Democratic candidate for Senate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at "The People v. The Powerful" rally at the Detroit Opera House on July 18, 2026. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)
El-Sayed then targeted the nation's healthcare system, arguing that medical debt should be eliminated and contrasting its cost with federal spending on political campaigns and foreign aid.
"Medical debt shouldn't exist," he said, claiming the country's roughly $225 billion in medical debt could be erased for about $2.25 billion because it can be purchased "for a penny on the dollar."
He later turned his attention to ICE, calling it a "rogue agency" that should not exist.

"ICE has nothing to do with immigration. ICE has nothing to do with the southern border. ICE is about normalizing paramilitary forces on our streets. ICE is about weaponizing the idea of immigration against the Constitution itself. ICE cannot be reformed. ICE cannot be retrained. ICE has to be abolished."
Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders joined Abdul El-Sayed during the final stop of "The People v. The Powerful" tour at DeVos Performance Hall in Grand Rapids. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Senate hopeful also described himself as "dangerous" to a range of political and corporate interests, including health insurers and Democratic leaders.
"If you're Blue Cross Blue Shield, I'm dangerous," he said. "If you're Chuck Schumer, trading politicians like trading cards, I'm dangerous."
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Anti-ICE walkout exposes how school district 'failed' parents, risked student safety: 'Broken my trust'
summary: Internal emails and texts show Flagstaff Unified School District staff allegedly knew about the ICE protest days in advance and helped students walk out.
story: Host Harris Faulkner and the 'Outnumbered' panel discuss U.S. high schools permitting students to walk out of class to protest ICE, despite low proficiency scores in math and English.

EXCLUSIVE: Internal emails, messages and memos from Arizona’s Flagstaff Unified School District (FUSD) reveal that staff allegedly breached security protocol and violated several school policies by facilitating a student walkout to protest U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) earlier this year, according to America First Legal.

Hundreds of Flagstaff high school and middle school students walked out of class to protest ICE on Jan. 28. The protest came amid national controversy over the deaths of anti-ICE activists Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota. Immediately after the walkout, many parents, citing safety concerns, expressed outrage that they were not notified that their children had been allowed to leave school premises without their consent. One parent who said they had children under the age of 12 said the "district failed us as parents."

Documents obtained by America First Legal, a conservative watchdog group, reveal that FUSD officials knew about the walkout days in advance and also coordinated with students. The documents, which were reviewed by Fox News Digital, were obtained by America First Legal through a lawsuit forcing FUSD to comply with its public records request for records related to the walkout.

Screenshots from a district staff text group show faculty coordinating during the walkout. One staff member texted, "We have 75 plus students staged outside of fhs [Flagstaff High School] getting ready to walk." In the same message, the staff member wrote, "Looks like we have some members of the public joining."
CONTROVERSIAL ICE TACTIC ACTUALLY REDUCES UNINTENDED 'COLLATERAL' ARRESTS: FEDERAL AGENT

Anti-ICE protesters attend a vigil for a man that was killed in a shooting involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), on July 13, 2026 in Biddeford, Maine. The victim has been identified as Joan Sebastian Guerrero, a 26-year-old man from Colombia. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)
Another concerning text from a staff member read, "Be aware of propped open doors that are left for reentry."

In response to America First Legal's criticism, a spokesperson for the district told Fox News Digital that "We respectfully disagree that the Flagstaff Unified School District encouraged students to attend or intentionally ignored District policies."
The spokesperson said, "The District was placed in the challenging position of balancing students’ First Amendment rights, student safety and school operations in the most appropriate way it could."

District policy dictates that "the Superintendent shall limit access to school buildings and grounds" and that faculty "maintain protocols regarding the distribution of keys or equipment to access District property." Further, FUSD policy also stipulates that students ages six to 16 are "required to attend school during the school's hours" and "the school in which the student is enrolled shall make a reasonable effort to promptly telephone and notify the parent/legal guardian or other person who has custody of the student of the student's absence from school."

An email from a student to then Flagstaff High School Principal Tadd Ragan shows that district staff was aware the protest would take place at least two days in advance. The student informed Ragan that students were planning to walk out of their classes to protest against ICE at 11:45 a.m. The student said the protest would occur "near a main road for more recognition" and asked for advice "in finding a more organized way of going about this."

In response, Ragan told the student that "as a District and School we have a plan to maintain a peaceful protest." In a subsequent email, Ragan asked the student, "Can you come by my office during first period?"

Another faculty member, Flagstaff "instructional coach" Janet Chavez-Vesely, sent an email to several school administrators the day before the protest, revealing that she had discussed the planned walkout with the student Hispanic Culture Club. Chavez-Vesely wrote that she "stayed neutral and answered questions while they planned."
VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT SUED OVER ALLEGED POLICY OF KEEPING STUDENTS' GENDER TRANSITIONS HIDDEN FROM PARENTS
Protesters gather in Austin, Texas, on January 8, 2026, to rally against ICE following the fatal shooting of Renee Nicole Good. (Stephanie Tacy/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

She noted that one of the students "plans to stop by and see me" to discuss the protest further. Chavez-Vesely told the school administrators, "I am available to support supervision," adding, "just let me know where."
Some parents who became aware of the walkout before it happened emailed the district, notifying staff that their children would be absent from school while citing safety concerns.

On Tuesday, one parent emailed Ragan, telling him, "I am keeping my daughter home from school this Wednesday as it has been brought to my attention that both Flagstaff high school and Coconino high school have planned out an entire protest."

The parent wrote, "This is not something that I want my child involved in nor do I want her around during it nor do I want her suffering any of the consequences that come with not participating and or being pressured into participating in potentially getting in a violent situation."

Another parent emailed faculty late on Tuesday night, writing, "My kids will not be at school tomorrow." The parent noted, "This is not something that I want my children exposed to or involved in as situations like this in the past have become violent and unsafe."
Meanwhile, at least one faculty member was excited about the protest, writing in a text, "This Walk out thing is going to be FUN!"

The morning of the protest, Sinagua Middle School Principal Christopher Koenker sent an email that FUSD "supports our students’ constitutional rights to peaceful assembly and free expression and is aware of student-led events planned."

He wrote that "schools will neither encourage nor discourage student participation." He added that the district was looking into providing additional staff and law enforcement presence "for protection and supervision, not to suppress student expression."
After the protest, an internal "Walk Out Debrief" memo emphasized that "school isn’t responsible for students’ safety after they leave campus."

Another memo noted that one teacher, identified as "Ms. Donovan," took her class outside to witness "rights vs. responsibilities" on display at the walkout. An administrator noted that just three students remained inside and that "later conversations with the 3 students indicated that they really weren’t comfortable being outside." The administrator noted she eventually asked Donovan to bring the class back inside "as it might appear that she was influencing them to be outside."
LAURA INGRAHAM: TEACHING US HISTORY HAS BECOME AN EXERCISE IN 'SELF-LOATHING AND RESENTMENT'

Twin Arrows, Arizona, The ruins of the Twin Arrows Trading Post, which closed in 1995. The building are now covered with graffiti, including a remembrance of Renee Good, who was killed by an ICE agent in Minneapolis in January 2026. (Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

In the same memo, the administrator noted that Donovan also discussed ICE operations in her class and had told students that officers had "used" a five-year-old "to lure the family out to take him." The administrator wrote that they had asked a student if she felt Donovan "pushes her opinions on her." The student answered that after the protest Donovan had asked students to raise their hands if they participated in the protest after which she "congratulated them," saying, "Great job for standing up for your first amendment rights."
Parents, however, quickly expressed that they felt outraged and blindsided.

One mother wrote that after learning of the protest, she and her husband "were terrified that our daughter was peer pressured (by friends, classmates, teachers, and the school district) to be a part of this."

"We’re thankful that our daughter remained at school, due to fear and frustration, but there is still the ‘what if’? What if something happened to any students during the walkout?" she continued, adding, "We expect the district to be transparent and not jeopardize our children’s safety."
A Las Vegas family says their son was expelled for posting pro-ICE stickers around campus following a student walkout protesting ICE. (Jason Armond / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Another middle school parent wrote that they were not made aware of the protest or contacted until the end of the day. They wrote that their child "was under the impression this was a school sponsored event," given that faculty allegedly provided "maps" and directions to the event.
"This school district has broken my trust and neglected your responsibilities and disregard for your own policies," the parent wrote.
Commenting on this, America First Legal Senior Counsel James Rogers told Fox News Digital that "What these documents show is a stunning betrayal of that trust."
Rogers said that FUSD’s "conduct raises serious questions about whether district employees crossed that line."
"Parents deserved to know where their children were. The law required these officials to act, and they failed on both counts," he said.
Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Hawley sends criminal referral of 'left-wing dark-money' group over mailed abortion drugs
summary: Sen. Josh Hawley alleges Plan C operates as a referral hub shipping abortion pills into states where they're banned, urging a criminal probe.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

FIRST ON FOX: A Republican senator says that a left-wing abortion group claiming to be a "public health information campaign" is actually operating as the referral hub for shipping abortion pills into states where they're banned, in a criminal referral obtained by Fox News Digital.

In a letter sent Thursday to acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, Sen. Josh Hawley alleges asked the Justice Department to open a criminal investigation into Plan C, saying the group connects women with abortion-pill manufacturers, foreign clinics and online vendors that ship the drugs into states where they are restricted by law.

"At the center of the effort is an entity called Plan C," Hawley wrote, describing the group as a "left-wing dark-money operation" that serves as the "referral and logistics hub" for distributing abortion drugs into states that prohibit them. He said the group's activities warrant a federal criminal investigation.
BLUE STATE SHIELD LAWS ALLOWED 330K ABORTION PILLS TO BE SENT TO ABORTION BAN STATES, PRO-LIFE GROUP FINDS
Sen. Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, is calling on the Justice Department to investigate Plan C. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Hawley says Plan C directs women in states such as Florida, Oklahoma and Texas to foreign clinics willing to mail abortion pills into the United States despite state laws restricting those shipments. He also says the group points users to online vendors selling abortion drugs without prescriptions, identification or medical consultations, even though Plan C acknowledges on its website that the pills sold through some of those sites are "not regulated or inspected by the US government."
Fox News Digital reached out to Plan C for comment.
Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)
Hawley's letter also says Plan C advises users on how to limit their "digital footprint" by recommending privacy-focused browsers, virtual private networks and encrypted email.

The senator notes that Plan C's own website warns users they could face legal consequences for obtaining abortion pills through the services it recommends, while saying it is "up to every individual to decide what level of legal risk they are willing to take."
HAWLEY URGES DOJ PROBE INTO ABORTION PILL MAKER OVER SAFETY CONCERNS

Hawley also says Plan C directs women to providers willing to prescribe abortion pills through 14 weeks of pregnancy — beyond the Food and Drug Administration's approved labeling for mifepristone and beyond the limits set by several states.
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., talks with reporters in the U.S. Capitol during votes related to the government shutdown on Thursday, Oct. 16, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Hawley argues the conduct could violate multiple federal laws, including provisions of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act covering prescription drugs, laws prohibiting the importation of unapproved drugs into interstate commerce, and federal conspiracy and aiding-and-abetting statutes.

"I therefore respectfully refer this matter to the Department to open a criminal investigation into Plan C, its relationship with potential co-conspirator manufacturers, and the network of suppliers it promotes," Hawley wrote, adding that the investigation should include foreign clinics and online vendors shipping abortion drugs into the United States.

title: FBI boss Kash Patel details how agency and partners secured record-shattering FIFA World Cup
summary: In a Fox News Digital exclusive, FBI Director Kash Patel details the massive World Cup security operation, including 700 drone takedowns and no significant attacks.
story: The FBI director details the massive security operation behind "78 Super Bowls in 38 days," including more than 700 drone takedowns and no significant criminal attacks. (Credit: Fox News Digital, Getty Images)

EXCLUSIVE – Seventy-eight Super Bowls in 38 days. This was the scale of the task facing the Federal Bureau of Investigation going into the first World Cup final the United States has hosted in more than 30 years."That’s what we executed on," FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview detailing the largest commitment of the agency’s resources ever devoted to securing a sporting event – the 2026 FIFA World Cup."We’re proud to report that, thank God, and thankfully to the men and women of the FBI and our partners, we had no significant criminal attacks during this World Cup," Patel said. "And just to put that in perspective, we had 6.5 million people attend the 78 matches in the U.S. across 11 venues."
Patel said the planning and execution had to be "mathematically precise."
FIFA WORLD CUP COMES TO THRILLING END WITH WINNING GOAL SCORED IN EXTRA TIME
Exclusive: FBI Director Kash Patel details how the agency and its partners secured the FIFA World Cup at FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C., on July 18, 2026. (Leigh Green for Fox News Digital)

The tournament shattered previous attendance records and brought millions of international visitors to the country. The FBI dedicated nearly 5,000 personnel to the effort, including more than 4,000 from field offices, 800 from FBI headquarters and two legal attaché offices, along with support from 59 Homeland Security task forces.

The bureau also conducted approximately 300,000 background checks on players, coaches and other accredited personnel. All told, nearly 7 million fans from all over the world attended World Cup games in the United States, Canada and Mexico, all with no reported major security incidents. In fact, getting into the stadiums often took fans less than 15 minutes for games that averaged more than 65,000 in house.

A defining element of the FBI’s security operation was its aggressive response to the rapidly evolving drone threat. Recognizing that even a low-cost unmanned aircraft could be used to surveil players practicing at the dozens of team base camps around the country, track their movements to and from hotels, probe for security tactics at stadiums or fan zones, disrupt an event or deliver an explosive or chemical device, the bureau treated every unauthorized incursion as a potential threat.
TRUMP TAKES IN JENNIFER HUDSON'S INCREDIBLE NATIONAL ANTHEM PERFORMANCE BEFORE WORLD CUP FINAL

Exclusive: FBI Director Kash Patel views a large screen filled with data inside the FBI's Intelligence Coordination Center. Patel praised the agency and its partners that helped secure a record-shattering World Cup. (Leigh Green for Fox News Digital)

"If you’re in the space, we’re gonna take you down. And that’s why we took down over 700," Patel said. "Some of these folks were maybe borderline nuisances, while many of them were criminal in terms of violations of FAA airspace and also failing to register their drones… We’re not taking any chances."

The FBI established its first dedicated counter-UAS (unmanned aircraft system) school at Redstone Arsenal in Alabama to train state and local officers in detecting, tracking and intercepting unauthorized drones. Those officers were then deployed on FBI-led ground-intercept teams at World Cup venues, creating a nationwide counter-drone capability built for a threat that barely existed when the U.S. last hosted the tournament in 1994.

Exclusive: FBI Director Kash Patel speaks with personnel at the agency's Intelligence Coordination Center. Patel praised the FBI and its partners for safely securing the World Cup. (Leigh Green for Fox News Digital)

"We, the FBI, specifically train for the worst of the worst," Patel said, pointing to the possibility of drones being used to deploy explosives or chemical agents. Former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino was instrumental in developing the bureau’s counter-drone program.
That preparation was tested as the World Cup was getting underway, when investigators uncovered an alleged coordinated attack targeting UFC Freedom 250 at the White House.
5 CHILLING DETAILS FROM THE ALLEGED WHITE HOUSE ATTACK PLOT TIED TO UFC EVENT
Exclusive: An FBI employee works inside the agency’s Intelligence Coordination Center, monitoring threats and coordinating security operations for the World Cup. (Leigh Green for Fox News Digital)

Federal prosecutors allege the suspects planned to use explosive-laden drones to trigger panic and force crowds to evacuate into areas where armed attackers could strike. Patel said the FBI launched a six-state operation, tracked the alleged threat through online communications and began a coordinated takedown "before the first punch was thrown," allowing the event to proceed without an attack.
Eight defendants have since been charged, although the allegations remain unproven and the defendants are presumed innocent.
FBI REVEALS WHY TRUMP WHITE HOUSE UFC EVENT WENT AHEAD DESPITE ALLEGED TERROR PLOT
International cooperation was another critical component of the World Cup security operation.
"They’re working overseas in their home locations and giving us information back in real time on any single threat that’s coming in," Patel said.
Exclusive: FBI Director Kash Patel interacts with personnel inside the agency's hub that was established to secure the World Cup. (Leigh Green for Fox News Digital)

The FBI hosted the International Police Cooperation Center in Northern Virginia, deploying more than 70 personnel to work alongside officers from U.S. host cities and security officials representing the nations sending teams to the tournament.

The FBI also assembled a Joint Operations Center with foreign police representatives from 46 of the 48 participating countries, allowing investigators to receive real-time threat intelligence from officials who understood their teams, fan bases and domestic security concerns. That information was supported by the FBI’s Intelligence Coordination Center, where more than 400 personnel processed an average of 26 incidents per day and produced nearly 100 intelligence reports for federal, state, local and private-sector partners, according to the FBI.

Patel credited the White House Task Force on the FIFA World Cup with bringing federal, state and local agencies together under a unified security strategy. Established by President Donald Trump and led by Andrew Giuliani’s team, the task force served as a central hub for interagency planning, intelligence sharing and the rapid deployment of law enforcement resources across the tournament’s 11 U.S. host cities.
FIRST WORLD CUP HALFTIME SHOW DRAWS MIXED REACTIONS FOR SHAKIRA, JUSTIN BIEBER, BTS, MADONNA PERFORMANCES

"Like anything in government, to succeed, you need tremendous leadership," Patel said. "President Trump had the foresight to establish the White House Task Force… and what they were able to do was bring in the interagency, at least at the federal level, and then work with us at the state and local levels through our partnerships and put everybody under one roof."

Patel said the coordinated structure allowed the FBI to quickly send bomb technicians, evidence teams, tactical operators, SWAT personnel and hostage-rescue capabilities wherever additional resources were needed.
FOX WORLD CUP ANNOUNCER SAYS TRUMP'S APPEARANCE AT FINAL IS 'FUN, UNIQUE THING' DESPITE POTENTIAL BACKLASH

"President Trump set the standard: Not only were we going to have the largest and safest sporting event in the history of the world, but we were going to make sure everyone had a great time. Those were the marching orders," Patel said.

He pointed to the social media videos showing international fans enjoying restaurants, pubs, sporting venues and other distinctly American experiences — even joking that Europeans fell in love with ranch dressing.

VIRAL GERMAN SOCCER FAN FREDDY INVITED FOR WHITE HOUSE VISIT AS FAIRY-TALE TRIP ACROSS AMERICA CONTINUES"These are small vignettes, but they quantify and qualify how awesome America did," Patel said. title: RNC trolls DNC, Maine Democratic Party in letter offering to help restore trust, 'defend democracy’
summary: The RNC sent a tongue-in-cheek letter offering election lawyers and trained observers to Democrats as Maine scrambles to replace Graham Platner.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The Republican National Committee is trolling the Democratic National Committee and the Maine Democratic Party with an offer to provide election lawyers, trained observers and other resources as Democrats scramble to replace disgraced Senate primary candidate Graham Platner.

"So, in a spirit of generosity we hope will not go unnoticed, the RNC formally offers our election integrity resources and personnel to ensure a process worthy of Democrat voters’ confidence," read a copy of the letter obtained exclusively by Fox News Digital. "Mainers deserve a nomination that is fair, accessible, and free from disenfranchisement — and it never hurts to have professionals in the room."

The tongue-in-cheek letter is expected to be sent Monday morning from the RNC to DNC chair Ken Martin and Maine Democratic Party Chair Charles Dingman, the RNC election integrity unit told Fox News Digital.
PLATNER ALLY TROY JACKSON CLOSING IN ON DEMOCRATIC SENATE NOD IN KEY RACE TO FACE COLLINS

From left, U.S. Senate candidates David Costello, Elizabeth Dickerson, Dan Kleban and Ashley Webb prepare for a televised debate at the WCSH-6 studio, Thursday, July 16, 2026, in Portland, Maine.  (AP Photo/Robert F. Bukaty)

The letter unwinds many of the Democratic Party platform's attacks on Republicans in a week that featured an unusual Democratic Party debate and President Donald Trump's primetime White House address on election integrity.

"The RNC has a deep bench of experienced election attorneys, trained observers, a dedicated State Election Integrity Director, and nationwide election integrity resources — all standing by to assist with convention procedures, delegate credentialing, ballot-counting transparency, and election law compliance," the letter read, pointing to its multi-million dollar midterm election integrity ground game. "We built this operation to protect elections from exactly this kind of chaos. We simply never expected the loudest cries for help to come from inside your own house.
"As our friends on the left never tire of reminding us, 'democracy dies in darkness.' We are offering to turn on the lights."
MEET THE DEMOCRATS GUNNING TO REPLACE GRAHAM PLATNER

Republicans have received criticism for questioning election integrity, but the RNC letter attempted to turn the table back on the Democrats, during a key Senate race in Maine that could help determine the Senate majority this November.

"We also request clarification on whether your nominating convention will include the basic safeguards every election deserves: voter identification, proof of residency, and independent observation," the letter continued, pointing to apparent hypocrisy. "We ask in a spirit of thoroughness, not suspicion. Mostly thoroughness."

"We further understand that proxy voting will not be permitted," the letter said. "I’m pleased to hear your party discover, at last, the merits of in-person voting — and to learn that when the stakes are highest for Democrats, you too believe there is no substitute for showing up and casting a ballot yourself."
When Platner suspended his Senate campaign before the July deadline after winning the nomination in June, he called out the party's "establishment" for forcing its will over the will of voters.

"For his part, Mr. Platner announced the suspension of his campaign by insisting that his replacement come from "'the people of Maine' through a system that is 'open, transparent and democratic' and that reflects the voices of those who supported him," the RNC letter noted, adding a dig on the DNC's reported financial struggles, suggesting its political opponents should accept their offer of help.
"We also know that this convention comes at a difficult time financially for you, with the DNC $18 million in debt. Finding the resources necessary to run a nominating convention must be tough."

title: RedHook Android malware can quietly hijack your phone
summary: RedHook Android malware abuses wireless debugging and accessibility permissions to gain shell-level control after victims sideload a malicious APK.
story: Halimah Delaine Prado, Google General Counsel, reveals the rise of AI-powered phishing scams originating from China's 'outsider enterprise.' She explains how these criminals use artificial intelligence to create highly convincing fake websites, impersonating trusted brands like T-Mobile to defraud hundreds of thousands of Americans, causing millions in losses. Prado highlights Google's strategy to combat these evolving threats.

Your phone rings, and the caller sounds official. They say your bank account or government service needs immediate verification. A link arrives moments later. The page looks like Google Play, and the caller tells you to install an app to fix the problem. Then the app asks you to turn on Accessibility access, a powerful Android permission that can let an app read the screen and control taps.

That approval can give the latest RedHook Android malware far more control than a regular app should have. Researchers at Group—IB, a global cybersecurity company that investigates online fraud and digital crime, analyzed the new threat. They say the upgraded remote access trojan, a type of malware that lets criminals control a device remotely, abuses Android's Wireless Debugging feature to gain shell-level privileges. That means it can run powerful system commands and change protected settings that ordinary apps cannot access, although it does not gain full root control.

RedHook can then watch the screen, record what you type, operate apps and steal login information. The new technique also helps it install or remove apps without showing the usual approval prompts. That makes one rushed permission decision especially costly.

NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS

Cybersecurity researchers warn that RedHook Android malware can seize extensive control of a phone after users install a malicious app and enable Accessibility permissions. (Chris Goodney/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
RedHook Android malware starts with a convincing scam

The attack begins with social engineering. Criminals call or message victims while posing as bank employees, government representatives or support agents. They direct people to fake websites that resemble official services or the Google Play Store. However, the app comes from outside Google Play. The victim sideloads an APK, which means installing an Android app from another source. After installation, the app guides the victim through enabling Accessibility.

Android built Accessibility services to help people use their devices. However, those services can also let an approved app observe the screen and perform actions for the user. RedHook takes advantage of that control. It simulates taps, opens Settings and enables Developer Options. Next, it turns on Wireless Debugging and asks Android for a pairing code.

The malware reads the code and connects back to the phone through 127.0.0.1, a local address that points to the same device. In effect, RedHook tricks the phone into connecting to its own powerful debugging controls, giving the malware deeper access without a computer.
Why Wireless ADB gives RedHook more control

ADB stands for Android Debug Bridge. Developers use it to manage a phone from a command line, install test apps and troubleshoot software. Android introduced Wireless Debugging with Android 11, allowing ADB connections over Wi-Fi instead of a USB cable. Once RedHook pairs with the phone, it gains shell-level access. That gives the malware more authority than a normal Android app, allowing it to run powerful commands and change protected settings. However, it still does not gain full root control.

RedHook can then grant itself additional permissions, capture low-level touch activity and avoid some confirmation screens that would normally alert the user. The malware also borrows from Shizuku, a legitimate Android utility used by developers and power users. Shizuku allows approved apps to use elevated Android features without rooting a phone. RedHook repurposes parts of that framework to carry out malicious commands.
What RedHook can do after it takes control
Group-IB counted 53 commands that attackers can send to the current RedHook version. Some commands appear unfinished, but the working features give criminals extensive access to an infected phone.

Attackers can stream the screen and capture screenshots.The malware records keystrokes and can collect screen-lock credentials.It can simulate taps, swipes, drags and long presses.Contacts, text messages and installed app lists can be collected.RedHook can install new APKs or remove apps without the usual prompts.Fake verification windows and black-screen overlays can hide its activity.The malware can activate a camera, including during a fake identity check.Remote commands can lock, unlock, wake or reboot the phone.
Attackers can stream the screen and capture screenshots.
The malware records keystrokes and can collect screen-lock credentials.
It can simulate taps, swipes, drags and long presses.
Contacts, text messages and installed app lists can be collected.
RedHook can install new APKs or remove apps without the usual prompts.
Fake verification windows and black-screen overlays can hide its activity.
The malware can activate a camera, including during a fake identity check.
Remote commands can lock, unlock, wake or reboot the phone.

That access creates several opportunities for fraud. A criminal could watch you sign in to a banking app, capture a verification code or place a convincing overlay above a real login screen. RedHook may also remove security software or install another malicious app.
RedHook uses several tricks to stay on your phone

Gaining access helps the attacker only while the malware remains active. Therefore, RedHook includes several persistence methods designed to keep Android from shutting it down. It can play silent audio so the operating system treats its process as important. A WakeLock keeps the CPU awake. Meanwhile, two separate services monitor each other and restart their partner when one stops.

RedHook also sets a five-minute alarm that checks whether its services remain alive. After a reboot, a receiver can restart the malware and reconnect its privileged helper. It even adjusts its out-of-memory score to reduce the chance that Android will close it when memory runs low. These methods make removal harder. They also explain why simply swiping the app away may accomplish very little.
Red flags to watch for before you tap Allow
One warning sign may have an innocent explanation. Several appearing together should make you stop and investigate.

A caller or message pressures you to install an app immediately.
The download page resembles Google Play, but it opens inside a web browser.
An app asks for Accessibility access without a clear need for it.
Instructions tell you to tap Build number seven times to enable Developer Options.
Wireless Debugging appears enabled although you never use developer tools.
A black overlay or fake system-update screen blocks your view.
An unfamiliar app keeps reopening or resists removal.
A bank or government representative asks you to install an APK from a link.
Do not let an urgent tone make the decision for you. Legitimate organizations can give you time to verify a request through an official phone number or website.
AMAZON RECALL TEXT SCAM COMES WITH RED FLAGS
A new version of RedHook malware exploits Android's Wireless Debugging feature, allowing attackers to steal data, control apps and monitor victims' devices. (Angel Garcia/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Ways to stay safe from RedHook Android malware
A few checks can stop this attack before it reaches the Wireless Debugging stage. Other steps can help limit the damage if you already installed a suspicious app.
Settings may vary depending on your Android phone’s manufacturer

Avoid APK files sent through texts, messaging apps or unexpected phone calls. Apps downloaded from unknown sources can put your device and personal information at risk. You should also review which apps can install software from outside Google Play. Open Settings and search for Install unknown apps . Turn off this permission for browsers, messaging apps and file managers unless you have a specific reason to use it.

Hang up and call the organization using the number printed on your bank card or listed on its official website. Avoid phone numbers included in the message, pop-up or download page. Be especially cautious when someone contacts you unexpectedly and pressures you to change a phone setting or install an app. Google lists both behaviors as warning signs of a possible scam.

Open Settings and search for Accessibility . Then review Installed apps , Downloaded apps or Installed services , depending on your phone. Turn off access for anything you do not recognize. An ordinary banking, delivery or government app rarely needs permission to read your screen and control your taps. Pause whenever an app claims that Accessibility access is required to complete verification. As CyberGuy has previously reported, malware can abuse Accessibility permissions to take control of an Android phone.

Open the Google Play Store > tap your profile icon > Play Protect . Tap Scan to check the apps currently installed on your phone. Play Protect may warn you about harmful software, which you can disable or remove from the phone. Google Play Protect, which is built-in malware protection for Android devices, automatically removes known malware. However, Play Protect may not catch every malicious app, so strong antivirus software adds another layer of protection.

Strong antivirus software can help flag malicious links, suspicious downloads and harmful apps. Keep its protection active, especially if you sometimes receive APK files for work or testing. However, do not assume an antivirus scan has fully removed RedHook if the app keeps returning or your settings continue to change. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com

Open Settings > Software updates , then follow the prompts. You can also check your Android security update and Google Play system update under About phone > Android version . Paths can differ slightly by device.

Turn on Airplane mode and use another trusted device to contact your bank and change important passwords. Do not enter more information on the affected phone. Try to remove the suspicious app or contact your phone manufacturer, carrier or a trusted repair professional for help. A factory reset may be necessary if the app returns or the phone continues behaving strangely.

A data removal service can help reduce the personal details available about you on people-search sites. That may include your home address, phone number and information about relatives. However, a data removal service cannot clean malware from your phone, recover stolen login information or remove data that criminals already copied. You can also submit opt-out requests yourself for free, although the process can take time. Information may later reappear, so continued monitoring may be needed. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com
HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER
Security experts say Android users should avoid sideloading apps and be cautious of unexpected requests to enable Accessibility or Developer Options. (Brent Lewin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

RedHook depends on social engineering before it can take control. The attacker still needs you to install a malicious app and approve powerful Accessibility permissions. That gives you a chance to stop the attack early. Be suspicious of urgent calls, fake app pages and anyone who tells you to install an APK from a link. Google Play Protect and strong antivirus software can help, but your best defense is slowing down before you approve an unexpected request.
Should Android make Accessibility permissions harder to approve when an app comes from outside Google Play? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: Amazon Leo satellite internet takes on Starlink
summary: Amazon Leo now has 396 satellites deployed after its July 2 launch, but Starlink's massive head start raises questions about when customers can sign up.
story: Kurt 'CyberGuy' Knutsson reveals common tactics used by ticket scammers during the World Cup, including fake websites, social media ads and AI-generated offers.

Amazon Leo satellite internet is getting closer to turning on service for customers. Amazon launched 29 more satellites into low Earth orbit on July 2, bringing its deployed total to 396 satellites, according to Amazon's latest mission update. That launch gives Amazon enough satellites for an initial service rollout later this year. However, the newest satellites still need to move into their assigned operating positions before they can support customers.

That is a big step for Amazon. It also shows how far Amazon still has to go. Starlink has been building its network since 2019 and already has a much larger satellite fleet, wider coverage and more paying customers. So, should Starlink be nervous? Maybe. Should you expect Amazon Leo to replace your home internet right away? Probably not yet.

Amazon’s planned Globalstar acquisition gives it spectrum, satellites and infrastructure to power satellite texting, calls and data beyond cell coverage. (Manuel Mazzanti/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
What is Amazon Leo satellite internet?

Amazon Leo is the new name for Project Kuiper, Amazon's low-Earth-orbit satellite internet network. Amazon says the goal is to deliver fast internet to customers and communities that lack reliable broadband. The name "Leo" comes from low Earth orbit. These satellites fly much closer to Earth than older satellite internet systems. That shorter distance can help reduce lag during video calls, streaming or online work.

Amazon says the network will use satellites, ground stations, fiber and customer antennas to connect people from space. The company also plans to offer different antennas for homes, businesses and other customers. In other words, Amazon wants Leo to become a serious internet option for places where cable, fiber or 5G home internet fall short.
Amazon Leo wraps Atlas V launches and moves to Vulcan

Amazon's July 2 mission was its 14th Leo launch. It was also the final launch in Amazon's Atlas V campaign with United Launch Alliance. Amazon says Atlas V launched 224 Leo satellites across eight missions with a 100% success rate. Now Amazon plans to move future ULA launches to the heavier Vulcan rocket, which can carry larger Leo payloads.

That change could help Amazon increase its deployment pace. Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo's director of launch systems, said the company has hundreds of flight-ready satellites waiting at Cape Canaveral. That detail stood out to me. Amazon may be late to the space internet race, but it clearly has hardware ready and a launch pipeline in motion.
Amazon Leo vs Starlink: where the race stands

Starlink still has the obvious lead. SpaceX started earlier, launched faster and already sells satellite internet in more than 150 countries, territories and markets, according to Starlink's availability map. Amazon Leo is at a very different stage. The company expects limited service later this year, with coverage and pricing still to come.

That means Starlink remains the more realistic choice if you need satellite internet today. Amazon Leo may become a stronger option later, especially if Amazon prices it aggressively or bundles it with business services. Still, I would not underestimate Amazon. The company has deep pockets, massive logistics experience and AWS, its cloud business, behind it. That combination could help Leo win customers in rural broadband, business connectivity, airlines and emergency backup systems.
Amazon Leo airline Wi-Fi plans

You may notice Amazon Leo on a plane before you see it on your roof. Amazon has already signed airline deals, including JetBlue and Delta. JetBlue plans to use Amazon's satellite technology to improve its free Fly-Fi service starting in 2027. Delta says Amazon Leo will roll out across hundreds of aircraft beginning in 2028, with an initial installation on 500 planes.

Amazon also introduced a commercial aviation antenna that it says can deliver speeds up to 1 Gbps down and 400 Mbps up. A single antenna can connect a full aircraft for entertainment, work and crew operations. That could make airline Wi-Fi feel much less painful. If Amazon can deliver stable service at cruising altitude, travelers will notice fast.
DAGEN MCDOWELL BLASTS BIG TECH FOR DATA-DRIVEN EFFICIENCY, IGNORING HUMAN COST

Amazon launched its second fleet of 27 Project Kuiper internet satellites in Cape Canaveral, Florida, on June 23, 2025, to create a mega constellation which will offer global broadband internet access. (Gregg Newton/AFP via Getty Images)
Amazon Leo direct-to-device phone service

Amazon also wants Leo to connect directly to phones and other cellular devices. That strategy became much bigger after Amazon announced plans to acquire Globalstar. Globalstar already supports satellite services used by Apple. Amazon says the deal will help Leo add direct-to-device services to future versions of its satellite network.

That could eventually help mobile carriers extend voice, text and data coverage beyond normal cell towers. Amazon also says its next-generation direct-to-device system will begin deploying in 2028. This could be very useful in dead zones, storms or emergencies. For now, though, treat satellite phone connectivity as backup coverage, not a full replacement for your carrier. If you want to prep your phone for emergencies now, check out this helpful guide on life-saving phone settings.
Why Amazon wants satellite internet customers

Satellite internet is becoming a much bigger business. Grand View Research estimates the global satellite internet market will grow from $13.3 billion in 2026 to $35.7 billion by 2033. That growth explains why Amazon wants in. Satellite internet can reach rural homes, farms, ships, planes, emergency teams and businesses that need backup connectivity.

Amazon also has a cloud advantage. Leo could connect directly with AWS services for companies that already rely on Amazon's cloud tools. That may give Amazon a stronger pitch for business customers than a regular home internet provider can offer. For everyday customers, the bigger benefit could be competition. Starlink, cable companies and 5G home internet providers may all have to work harder if Amazon becomes a serious broadband rival.
How to compare satellite internet before you switch

If Amazon Leo becomes available in your area, do not focus only on the name. Compare it the same way you would compare any internet service. Start with monthly price, equipment cost and installation needs. Then check download speed, upload speed, latency and data limits. You should also look at cancellation terms, customer support and whether the service works well in bad weather.

That last part is important. Satellite internet can be a lifesaver in places without reliable wired service. However, trees, storms and placement can affect performance. If you are already comparing providers, check out our article on how to get high speed internet at a discount rate. You can also review this breakdown of 5G home internet vs cable before you make a switch.
What this means to you

If you live in an area with poor internet choices, Amazon Leo could eventually give you more leverage. That alone is good news. Still, I would wait for Amazon to publish coverage maps, monthly pricing and real customer performance before getting too excited. A rocket launch is impressive, but your internet bill and actual speed at home matter more.

If you fly often, Leo may show up first as better in-flight Wi-Fi. JetBlue and Delta give Amazon a very public test. If the service feels fast and reliable in the air, that could build trust fast. For your phone, direct-to-device satellite service could become an emergency safety net. It may help when you are hiking, driving through a dead zone or stuck during a major outage.

At home, Amazon Leo could also push your current internet provider to improve. If you are dealing with slow speeds now, my tips on how to speed up your Wi-Fi and internet connection are a good place to start while Leo builds out.
JEFF BEZOS REPORTEDLY TOLD TRUMP THE WASHINGTON POST WAS HIS ‘WORST INVESTMENT’ BEFORE STAFF CUTS
Amazon is making a major satellite push with Globalstar, aiming to challenge Starlink and expand direct-to-device connectivity for remote users. (Manuel Mazzanti/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

Amazon Leo has moved from an idea to a real satellite network with 396 satellites deployed, airline deals lined up and a direct-to-device phone strategy in the works. Still, Starlink has the lead today. It has more satellites, broader coverage and years of customer experience behind it. If you need satellite internet right now, Starlink is the one you can actually buy in many places. That said, I would not count Amazon out. Jeff Bezos knows how to enter a crowded market and make competitors sweat. If Amazon Leo forces better prices, faster service or more coverage, you could benefit even if you never put an Amazon antenna on your roof.
Would you trust Amazon to run your internet from space, or would you wait until Leo proves it can truly compete with Starlink? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: How sweepstakes entry data can reach scammers
summary: Sweepstakes entry data can fuel marketing profiles and reach scammers. The Epsilon fraud case revealed how targeted lists harmed older adults.
story: Smart refrigerators, cars and computers can show ads after updates, raising privacy and ownership concerns, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

It's summer. Mall kiosks promise free cruises. Retailers run drawings at checkout. Entry cards sit in stacks near the register. You fill one out, drop it in the box and forget about it by the time you reach your car.

That may be the last moment the information feels contained. Many sweepstakes are legitimate. Still, the official rules or privacy policy may allow the sponsor, its affiliates or marketing partners to use and share your information. The privacy risk grows when those details become part of a larger marketing profile, move through the data broker industry or reach buyers running deceptive campaigns.

Join us Wednesday, July 22, at 1 p.m. ET for a free CyberGuy Live class that will help you cut down on robocalls, spam texts, junk email and other unwanted messages. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will walk you step by step through simple ways to filter spam, clean up your inbox and recognize the messages that could put your personal information at risk. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our spam—stopping checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

FCC ROBOCALL CRACKDOWN COULD CHANGE PHONE PRIVACY
A simple sweepstakes form can collect personal details that later become part of a larger marketing profile.  (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What personal information sweepstakes collect

A basic sweepstakes entry may ask for your name, email address and phone number. Some promotional forms request far more, including your age range, household income, health interests, medications or magazine subscriptions. Those extra questions can have marketing value even when they have little connection to selecting a winner.

The Federal Trade Commission has found that data brokers collect information from online and offline sources, including purchases, magazine subscriptions, income data and other personal details. Brokers can combine those records into profiles that help marketers predict what may capture your attention.
Before entering, ask yourself whether the sponsor truly needs each answer. The more information you provide, the more detailed the resulting profile can become.
How sweepstakes entry data becomes a marketing profile

Responding to a sweepstakes can become a valuable signal. It tells a marketer that a prize—based offer caught your attention and persuaded you to provide personal information. The FTC has warned that sweepstakes promoters may sell entry information to advertisers. That can lead to more targeted advertising, junk mail, telemarketing calls and spam.

Your entry may also be combined with purchase histories, demographic estimates and records collected from other sources. As a result, the profile can reveal far more than the few answers written on the original form. Once you are categorized as someone who responds to sweepstakes, your information may become more valuable to companies promoting similar offers. The danger grows when a poorly controlled list reaches a buyer running a fraudulent campaign.
What the Epsilon fraud case revealed

Epsilon Data Management was one of the world's largest marketing companies. It entered a deferred prosecution agreement with the Justice Department after acknowledging that one of its business units sold consumer lists to mass-mailing fraud schemes. Those operations sent false sweepstakes notices and astrology solicitations. The mailings claimed recipients had won prizes or could receive personalized psychic services after paying a fee. People who paid received nothing of value.

Epsilon agreed to pay $150 million in penalties and victim compensation. Of that amount, $127.5 million was designated for people harmed by fraud schemes that used Epsilon data. Many of the people targeted were older adults. The case continued beyond the company settlement. A jury later convicted a former Epsilon executive and sales manager of conspiracy, mail fraud and wire fraud.

The Justice Department said the defendants sold targeted lists to fraudsters who used them to identify people likely to respond to deceptive mailings. The case documents a specific abuse of targeted marketing data rather than a universal path for every sweepstakes entry. Still, it shows how information collected for marketing can become a road map for fraud when it reaches the wrong buyer.
Sweepstakes entry data can lead to more promotional mail and convincing fake prize notices. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How sweepstakes entry data can reach scammers
The exact path will vary by promotion. However, one possible chain looks like this:

You enter a sweepstakes and provide your contact information.The sponsor stores the entry and uses or shares it according to the official rules and privacy policy.A marketing company combines your answers with information from other sources.Your record becomes part of a segment based on your interests and response history.The information passes to additional marketers or data brokers.In the worst cases, a buyer uses the list to send deceptive prize notices or other targeted scams.
You enter a sweepstakes and provide your contact information.
The sponsor stores the entry and uses or shares it according to the official rules and privacy policy.
A marketing company combines your answers with information from other sources.
Your record becomes part of a segment based on your interests and response history.
The information passes to additional marketers or data brokers.
In the worst cases, a buyer uses the list to send deceptive prize notices or other targeted scams.
This chain can unfold without a malicious website, infected attachment or stolen password. The starting point may be a paper form sitting inside a familiar store.
Why local sweepstakes can create privacy risks

A mall kiosk or retailer drawing feels safer than a random website because you recognize the location. That familiarity can make the privacy terms easier to overlook. Before entering, look for the official rules and privacy policy. Check whether the sponsor can share your data with affiliates, sponsors or marketing partners.

Also watch for language giving permission to call, email or text you. Once several companies receive the information, tracing every copy becomes difficult. That lack of visibility is one reason a simple contest entry can create a much larger privacy footprint.
Older adults may receive targeted prize offers designed to feel personal, urgent and legitimate. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect your sweepstakes entry data
A few simple habits can limit the information you hand over, reduce unwanted marketing and help your family recognize a fake prize before money changes hands.
You cannot pull back every sweepstakes entry you have already submitted. However, you can reduce the amount of personal information available through data brokers and people-search sites.

Start by searching for your name, phone number, email address and home address online. You may find profiles that reveal your age, relatives, past addresses and other personal details. Many data brokers provide an opt-out process, although removing your information manually can take time and may require repeated requests.

You can also use a reputable data removal service to contact brokers on your behalf and continue submitting removal requests when your information reappears. Before signing up, check how many brokers the service covers, whether it offers ongoing monitoring and whether you can request removals from specific sites.

No service can erase every public record, social media post or privately held database. Still, reducing the number of sites displaying and selling your information can make it harder for marketers and scammers to build a detailed profile about you.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web: CyberGuy.com.

Provide the minimum information required for a valid entry. Think twice when a form asks about your income, medications, health concerns, shopping habits or other sensitive subjects. Some promotions need your age or date of birth to verify eligibility. However, questions unrelated to the official requirements may serve a marketing purpose.
WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME

Look for the sponsor's full name, eligibility requirements, drawing date and privacy terms. Pay close attention to language explaining whether your information may be shared with affiliates or marketing partners. When no official rules or identifiable sponsor appear, skip the promotion.

Watch for preselected boxes or fine print that gives the sponsor permission to send promotions by email, phone or text. Leave optional marketing boxes unchecked. When consent is required to enter, decide whether the prize feels worth the additional contact and data sharing.

Consider creating an alias email address used only for contests, store loyalty programs and promotional offers. This makes follow-up marketing easier to recognize and keeps your primary inbox less exposed. A separate address cannot prevent the sponsor from sharing the information you provide. However, it can help you contain the resulting email. For more ways to protect your inbox, read how your email address gets into the wrong hands.

Do not provide a bank account number, credit card number or payment app information on a sweepstakes entry. The Postal Inspection Service advises consumers to avoid any sweepstakes requesting financial information or payment. A legitimate sponsor may need tax information after you have independently verified a major prize. That request should come after the drawing and through a confirmed company contact rather than on the original entry form.

Take a photo of a paper entry form or save a screenshot of an online promotion. Keep the official rules, sponsor name and drawing date. When someone later claims you won, compare the message with the original promotion. Contact the sponsor through information you find independently rather than using a phone number or link provided in the prize message.

The Epsilon schemes harmed many older adults and other vulnerable people. Watch for prize letters that feel urgent, personal or unusually persistent. Talk with parents and grandparents before a suspicious letter arrives. Make sure they know to call someone they trust before sending money or personal information. You can also share our guide on how to stop scam texts from targeting aging parents.

Real prizes are free. A demand for taxes, processing costs, shipping fees, gift cards, cryptocurrency or a money transfer signals a scam. Scammers often create urgency, so you have less time to question the story. Slow down and verify the company yourself. Gift card demands deserve special caution. CyberGuy has also covered how fake prizes lead to gift card losses.

Legitimate marketing emails must provide a way to opt out of future messages. Use the unsubscribe option when you recognize the company and remember signing up. Avoid clicking unsubscribe links inside suspicious messages. A fake link may lead to a phishing page or confirm that your email address remains active. Mark the message as spam and block the sender instead.

Report suspected prize or sweepstakes scams at the Federal Trade Commission's ReportFraud.ftc.gov. You can file a report even when you spotted the scam before losing money. When the scam involves the U.S. Mail, report it to the U.S. Postal Inspection Service at uspis.gov/report. The agency accepts reports involving sweepstakes, lottery and other mail fraud.
COULD THE 7-ELEVEN BREACH AFFECT YOU?
Kurt's key takeaways

That little entry card by the register can reveal far more than you think. The real concern begins when extra details leave the sponsor and become part of a marketing profile that gets shared, categorized and sold. The Epsilon case showed how lists of likely responders can become a road map for fraud, with older adults paying a steep price. Give the minimum, skip optional marketing consent and read the privacy terms before you enter. Then talk with the older people in your life before a convincing prize letter reaches their mailbox. Any prize notice demanding money belongs in the trash. You cannot pull back every old entry, but you can shrink your data trail and make your household harder to target.

title: Would this survival pod make you feel safer?
summary: LifePods survival capsules from Momentum Technologies offer flood, ballistic and earthquake protection starting around $27,000 before shipping costs.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Disaster prep used to mean bottled water, flashlights and maybe a generator in the garage. Now a French startup is taking all of that to the next level. Momentum Technologies recently showed off its LifePods survival capsules. According to the company's website, the capsules are designed to protect people, families, response teams and critical infrastructure during natural disasters, industrial risks and security threats.

You can see why something like this would get a lot of attention right now. Blackouts seem more common. Floods can move fast. Global instability has many of you wondering how prepared you really are if help cannot get there right away. LifePods takes that fear and turns it into a physical product you can buy, move and place before disaster hits.
